correctness.rationale: A fresh reconstruction from the Fano-plane incidence rule independently found 154 independent triples and 15,900 faces including the empty face, with the stated nonempty face vector. Replaying the sequential element matching gave 7,932 pairs and exactly 36 unmatched faces, all of dimension eight, with the empty face matched. Independently orienting every one of the 109,410 Hasse cover relations downward except for reversed matched edges produced an acyclic directed graph. Thus the matching is a complete discrete-Morse certificate with one implicit 0-cell and 36 critical 8-cells, proving the wedge homotopy type. The package's mod-2 chain-rank computation is consistent but is not used as a substitute for the homotopy certificate.
correctness.risk: The conclusion is exact for this finite graph and k=3 only.

originality.rationale: The defining Bayer et al. paper was inspected in full. Its explicit bipartite homotopy formula is for complete bipartite graphs \(K_{m,n}\), and its other general exact theorem is for chordal graphs; the Heawood graph is neither complete bipartite nor chordal. Full-text searches found no Heawood, projective-plane or incidence-graph case. The later primary paper focuses on total 2-cut complexes of cycle powers and specified Cartesian products, so it does not cover k=3 Heawood. Resultary searches located only the audited record for this exact object.

value.rationale: The Heawood graph is the canonical Levi graph of the Fano plane and a standard highly symmetric nonchordal bipartite test case. An exact homotopy decomposition outside the graph families treated by the defining theory is a natural finite topological benchmark, and the result supplies a complete Morse certificate rather than only a Betti-number census.
value.risk: No family-level Levi-graph theorem is obtained.

final_claim: For the Heawood graph \(H\), the total \(3\)-cut complex satisfies \(\Delta_3^t(H)\simeq\bigvee^{36}S^8\).
limitations: Heawood graph and total k=3 only.
No extrapolation to projective-plane incidence graphs of higher order.
